										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at <strong>KU Leuven</strong>, <strong>Kunsan National University</strong>, <strong>Vrije Universiteit Brussel</strong>, <strong>imec,</strong> et al. published “Irradiation-Source-Dependent Tone Conversion in Dry-Deposited Halogenated Amorphous Zeolitic Imidazolate Framework Resists for Electron-Beam and Extreme Ultraviolet Lithography.”</p>
<p><strong>Abstract Excerpt:</strong><br />
“Dry-deposited metal–organic resists are key enablers for advanced patterning processes in next-generation semiconductor manufacturing. Here, we report halogenated amorphous zeolitic imidazolate framework (a-ZIF) resists deposited entirely by a dry process, which exhibit a pronounced irradiation-source-dependent tone conversion.&#8221;</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Researchers from <strong>Institute of Science Tokyo, Yokohama National University</strong>, <strong>AIST</strong>, and <strong>Photonics Electronics Technology Research Association</strong> (PETRA) published a technical paper titled “Reduced-DSP 200G/λ Low-Voltage Slow-Light Silicon Modulator Enabled by Built-In EO Equalizer.”</p>
<p><strong>Abstract Excerpt:</strong></p>
<p>“Multi-Tb/s optical interconnects for artificial intelligence data centers necessitate high-speed, energy-efficient, and compact transceivers. However, conventional silicon Mach-Zehnder modulators are fundamentally limited by low modulation efficiency and large physical dimensions that typically extend several millimeters, requiring high-swing drivers and power-intensive digital signal processing to achieve data rates exceeding 100 Gb/s per lane. Here we show a silicon photonic crystal waveguide slow-light modulator that overcomes the bandwidth-efficiency trade-off via a built-in electro-optic equalizer.&#8221;</p>
<p>Find the <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-78128-1">technical paper here</a>. October 2026</p>
<p>Kawahara, K., Tsuchizawa, T., Yamamoto, N. et al.Reduced-DSP 200G/λ low-voltage slow-light silicon modulator enabled by built-in EO equalizer. Nat Commun 17, 10446 (2026). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78128-1.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/silicon-photonic-modulator-reaches-200-gb-s-pam4-with-reduced-dsp-science-tokyo-yokohama-aist-petra/">Silicon Photonic Modulator Reaches 200 Gb/s PAM4 With Reduced DSP (Science Tokyo, Yokohama, AIST, PETRA)</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at Arizona State University and University of Maryland published “SEAL: Multitenant Security-Aware Layer Mapping for Heterogeneous 3-D CiM Accelerators.” Abstract: &#8220;Heterogeneous 3-D compute-in-memory architectures can combine different memory technologies across stacked tiers to accelerate deep neural network inference, but multitenant deployments introduce security risks through shared power delivery networks. The researchers developed SEAL, a security-aware... <a class="read_more" href="https://semiengineering.com/security-aware-layer-mapping-reduces-fault-vulnerability-in-3d-compute-in-memory-asu-u-of-maryland/">&#187; read more</a></p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/security-aware-layer-mapping-reduces-fault-vulnerability-in-3d-compute-in-memory-asu-u-of-maryland/">Security-Aware Layer Mapping Reduces Fault Vulnerability In 3D Compute-In-Memory (ASU, U. of Maryland)</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at <strong>Arizona State University</strong> and <strong>University of Maryland</strong> published “SEAL: Multitenant Security-Aware Layer Mapping for Heterogeneous 3-D CiM Accelerators.”</p>
<p><strong>Abstract</strong>:<br />
&#8220;Heterogeneous 3-D compute-in-memory architectures can combine different memory technologies across stacked tiers to accelerate deep neural network inference, but multitenant deployments introduce security risks through shared power delivery networks. The researchers developed SEAL, a security-aware layer-mapping framework that jointly optimizes power, performance, area, and fault vulnerability by assigning critical neural-network layers to more fault-resilient device and tier combinations. Evaluations using ResNet-18 and Qwen2.5-3B showed reductions in fault vulnerability of up to 3.9× and 7.8×, respectively, compared with security-blind mapping where both approaches produced usable mappings. In ReRAM-heavy configurations, SEAL placed all high-criticality layers on low-vulnerability tiers and reduced fault vulnerability to the characterization floor. ResNet-18 accuracy remained within 0.06 percentage points of the fault-free baseline, while Qwen2.5-3B perplexity remained within 0.06 of its fault-free baseline.&#8221;</p>
<p>Find the <a href="https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11692886">technical paper here</a>. September 2026</p>
<p>Sharma, Pragya, Sriniketh Purisai Ramanujam, Ashish Reddy Bommana, Hossein Pourmehrani, Naghmeh Karimi, Farshad Firouzi, and Krishnendu Chakrabarty. “SEAL: Multitenant Security-Aware Layer Mapping for Heterogeneous 3-D CiM Accelerators.” IEEE Journal on Exploratory Solid-State Computational Devices and Circuits, September 2026. https://doi.org/10.1109/JXCDC.2026.3734047. <a href="https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">License</a>.</p>

		<title>Neural Networks Speed 3nm Nanosheet SPICE Simulation (TU Munich)</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/neural-networks-speed-3nm-nanosheet-spice-simulation-tu-munich/</link>

		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Technical Paper Link]]></dc:creator>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at Technical University of Munich published “NN-Based Transistor Modeling for Ultra-Fast SPICE Simulation and Standard Cell Library Characterization.” Abstract: “Neural network (NN)-based transistor models have proven to be a promising solution to accelerate device modeling. Although these models demonstrated remarkable speedup in circuit simulations, they were not rigorously tested in complex tasks within standard... <a class="read_more" href="https://semiengineering.com/neural-networks-speed-3nm-nanosheet-spice-simulation-tu-munich/">&#187; read more</a></p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/neural-networks-speed-3nm-nanosheet-spice-simulation-tu-munich/">Neural Networks Speed 3nm Nanosheet SPICE Simulation (TU Munich)</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>Researchers at <strong>Technical University of Munich</strong> published “NN-Based Transistor Modeling for Ultra-Fast SPICE Simulation and Standard Cell Library Characterization.”</p>
<p><strong>Abstract</strong>:<br />
“Neural network (NN)-based transistor models have proven to be a promising solution to accelerate device modeling. Although these models demonstrated remarkable speedup in circuit simulations, they were not rigorously tested in complex tasks within standard EDA tool flows for chip design, which require very high transistor model precision to provide accurate results and converge properly. To investigate their full potential and promise, we develop NN-based transistor models that accurately predict the drain current and various charges for a 3nm nanosheet, and employ the models for a standard cell library characterization. This enables us to evaluate the accuracy and speedup under a very wide range of SPICE simulations, benchmarking our models against an industry-standard implementation. Since standard cell library characterization involves thousands of SPICE simulations, it serves as a great benchmark for transistor model quality and consistency. To further evaluate model accuracy, we also perform analog- and digital-level simulations for various complex circuits. Our experiments reveal that NN-based models are a valid alternative to existing transistor compact models, capable of producing accurate delay and power estimates with a much higher speed and convergence time compared to the conventional Verilog-A-based industry-standard (BSIM-CMG) transistor compact model. Our NNs achieve sub-0.11% and 0.76% errors for delay and total power evaluation on a wide range of circuits, while taking up to 8 times less time during the standard cell library characterization. Additionally, we provide comprehensive information and guidance on NN accuracy, unveiling the relationship between NN size and its effect on circuit simulation precision.”</p>
<p>Find the <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31024">technical paper here</a>. October 2026</p>
<p>Novkin, Rodion, and Hussam Amrouch. “NN-Based Transistor Modeling for Ultra-Fast SPICE Simulation and Standard Cell Library Characterization.” arXiv, October 2026. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.31024. <a href="https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">License</a></p>
<p>&nbsp;</p>

										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<h3><strong>CHIPS Act funding</strong></h3>
<p>The <strong>U.S. Commerce Department</strong> signed letters of intent for up to $389M in <a href="https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/10/department-commerce-announces-letters-intent-4-companies-389-million-rd">semiconductor R&amp;D funding</a> to four companies working on power devices and critical materials, including vertical GaN and ultra-high-purity quartz technologies. Under the proposed agreements, the government will receive minority, nonvoting equity stakes as a condition of the awards.</p>

<h3 role="heading" aria-level="2" data-uw-rm-heading="level"><strong>Manufacturing capacity</strong></h3>
<p><strong>Nvidia</strong> expanded <a href="https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-and-supply-chain-partners-expand-capacity-to-accelerate-ai-infrastructure-buildout">capacity agreements across its manufacturing supply chain</a>, including deals with:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Amkor</strong> to expand <a href="https://ir.amkor.com/news-releases/news-release-details/amkor-technology-and-nvidia-advance-strategic-partnership-aim">advanced packaging capacity</a> in S. Korea, bringing the companies&#8217; combined Arizona and S. Korea agreements to $3B. The expansion targets more than a fourfold increase in interposer wafer capacity by the end of 2028.</li>
<li><strong>SPIL</strong> to expand <a href="https://www.spilglobal.com/NewsDetail/d968ea095a2d08fe">optical-engine assembly capacity for CPO</a> in Taiwan;</li>
<li><strong>Samsung Electro-Mechanics</strong> to expand <a href="https://www.samsungsem.com/global/newsroom/news/view.do?id=10614">ABF package substrate production</a> in S. Korea;</li>
<li><strong>KYEC</strong> to build new <a href="https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-and-supply-chain-partners-expand-capacity-to-accelerate-ai-infrastructure-buildout">semiconductor testing facilities</a> in the U.S., with a $1.1B advance;</li>
<li><strong>IBIDEN</strong> to expand <a href="https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-and-supply-chain-partners-expand-capacity-to-accelerate-ai-infrastructure-buildout">package substrate capacity</a> in Japan;</li>
<li><strong>Unimicron</strong> to increase <a href="https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-and-supply-chain-partners-expand-capacity-to-accelerate-ai-infrastructure-buildout">package substrate production</a> in Taiwan.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Advanced packaging and inspection</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>UMC</strong> and <strong>AP Memory</strong> announced a technology and manufacturing collaboration to develop silicon-capacitor <a href="https://www.umc.com/en/News/press_release/Content/technology_related/20261022">power-delivery solutions</a> for AI and HPC systems, using UMC’s deep-trench-capacitor technology to move capacitance from the board into the interposer, substrate, or landside of advanced packages.</li>
<li>As advanced packaging scales, a new report examines the <a href="https://semiengineering.com/what-breaks-when-packaging-moves-from-wafer-to-panel/">challenges of moving from wafer to panel</a>, including warpage, yield, process control, and equipment limitations.</li>
<li><strong>Siemens</strong> and <strong>Nvidia</strong> expanded <a href="https://news.siemens.com/en-us/siemens-nvidia-gtc-3d-ic-thermal-ai/">agentic AI for 3D-IC</a> electrothermal co-design, with Siemens reporting up to 95% less engineering effort and 50× more design alternatives. The companies are also developing a <a href="https://news.siemens.com/en-us/siemens-nvidia-pcba-digital-twin-factory/">PCB inspection digital twin</a> using virtual boards and synthetic defect data to reduce manual engineering effort by up to 85% and false calls by more than 40%.</li>
</ul>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" class="alignnone wp-image-24283174" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-21-at-4.15.33-PM.png?resize=600%2C380&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="600" height="380" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-21-at-4.15.33-PM.png?resize=300%2C190&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-21-at-4.15.33-PM.png?resize=600%2C380&amp;ssl=1 600w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-21-at-4.15.33-PM.png?w=645&amp;ssl=1 645w" sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 600px" /><br />
<strong>Fig.1: </strong><b>Agentic 3D IC engineering workflow aimed at power and thermal challenges. Source: Siemens</b></p>
<h3><strong>AI data center power delivery</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Infineon</strong> and <strong>Nvidia</strong> expanded their collaboration on 800 VDC power architectures for AI data centers, focusing on <a href="https://www.infineon.com/press-release/2026/infpr202610-012">GaN-based intermediate bus converters</a> (IBCs) designed to improve power efficiency and density for high-power AI systems.</li>
<li>Explore the <a href="https://semiengineering.com/800vdc-pushes-ai-power-design-from-grid-to-gate/">shift to 800 VDC power delivery</a> in AI data centers and the <a href="https://semiengineering.com/what-can-go-wrong-in-800vdc-ai-data-centers/">safety and reliability challenges</a> posed by higher-voltage architectures.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Standards</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Advanced Photonics Coalition</strong> released its first portfolio of five specifications and recommended practices for <a href="https://www.advanced-photonics.org/apc-documents-press-release">silicon photonics and co-packaged optics</a>.</li>
<li><strong>Accellera</strong> released <a href="https://www.accellera.org/news/press-releases/432-accellera-approves-functional-safety-language-standard-1-0-for-release">Functional Safety Language Standard 1.0</a>, providing a common data model for exchanging and reusing functional-safety information across design tools and teams, with an initial focus on standardizing FMEDA data exchange.</li>
</ul>
<h3 role="heading" aria-level="2" data-uw-rm-heading="level"><strong>China</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Samsung Electronics</strong> and <strong>SK hynix</strong> reportedly are upgrading their <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/china/samsung-sk-hynix-upgrading-china-plants-make-more-advanced-chips-people-say-2026-10-21/">China NAND fabs</a> to produce more advanced memory, with Samsung targeting 286-layer V9 NAND production in Xi’an and SK hynix moving toward 240-layer or higher NAND in Dalian, despite U.S. restrictions on chipmaking equipment exports, according to Reuters.</li>
<li><strong>ByteDance</strong>, <strong>Alibaba</strong>, and <strong>Tencent</strong> have reportedly placed more than <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/retail-consumer/bytedance-alibaba-tencent-place-over-35-billion-worth-nvidia-chip-orders-2026-10-20/">$35B in orders</a> for Nvidia’s export-compliant RTX PRO 5500 GPUs, according to Reuters.</li>
<li role="heading" aria-level="2" data-uw-rm-heading="level">China&#8217;s access to <a href="https://ifp.org/how-to-increase-americas-ai-lead-over-china/">AI computing power could nearly double</a> to 8.8M Nvidia H100 equivalents by the end of 2027, <strong>IFP</strong> estimates, although tighter chip export controls and restrictions on overseas data-center access could slow growth.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Memory</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Micron</strong> outlined a <a href="https://s25.q4cdn.com/621799436/files/doc_downloads/2026/10/MU-TP-Webinar.pdf">memory technology roadmap</a> featuring vertical HBM stacked directly on compute, targeting volume production in 2028. Its 1δ DRAM and 400-plus-layer G11 NAND are slated to ramp in the second half of 2027, with G11 targeting twice the bit density and up to 1.5× the I/O speed of G9.</li>
<li><strong>JEDEC</strong> established a new task group to explore an <a href="https://www.everspin.com/news/everspin-technologies-chair-new-jedecr-task-group-exploring-lpddr-persistent-memory-standard">LPDDR persistent-memory (PMEM)</a> standard.</li>
<li><strong>Samsung</strong> reportedly will use <strong>TSMC</strong>’s <a href="https://en.sedaily.com/finance/2026/10/18/samsung-to-tap-tsmc-3-nanometer-lines-for-nvidia-custom-hbm">3nm process for the base die in Nvidia’s custom NVHBM</a>, while continuing to manufacture the DRAM dies itself. Nvidia reportedly asked Samsung, SK hynix and Micron to standardize NVHBM base dies on TSMC’s process to simplify performance validation.</li>
<li><strong>Indium</strong> is expanding its Rome, New York, operations to restart U.S. processing of high-purity critical <a href="https://micron.gcs-web.com/news-releases/news-release-details/micron-invests-new-york-critical-minerals-processing-indium">materials used in advanced memory manufacturing</a>, backed by an investment and long-term supply agreement with <strong>Micron</strong>.</li>
</ul>
<h3 role="heading" aria-level="2" data-uw-rm-heading="level"><strong>Funding</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Tenstorrent</strong> <a href="https://tenstorrent.com/newsroom/tenstorrent-announces-series-e">raised $1.5B</a> in Series E funding to scale manufacturing and deployment of its Galaxy servers and advance its AI and RISC-V CPU IP.</li>
<li><strong>Photon Bridge</strong> raised about $11M to develop scalable multi-wavelength <a href="https://www.photonbridge.com/news/photon-bridge-raises-%E2%82%AC10m-to-tackle-ai%E2%80%99s-emerging-laser-bottleneck">laser sources for optical interconnects</a> in AI data centers.</li>
</ul>
<h3 role="heading" aria-level="2" data-uw-rm-heading="level"><strong>Earnings</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li>Notable: <strong>Lam Research</strong> reported record quarterly revenue of <a href="https://newsroom.lamresearch.com/2026-10-21-Lam-Research-Corporation-Reports-Financial-Results-for-the-Quarter-Ended-September-27,-2026">$8.2B, up 54% YoY</a>, with systems revenue rising 62% to $5.7B amid strong AI-driven wafer-fab equipment demand.</li>
<li>Quarterly Revenue: <a href="https://www.marketscreener.com/news/be-semiconductor-industries-n-announces-q3-2026-results-ce785cd9de89ff27">Besi</a> (up 114%), <a href="https://www.prnewswire.com/apac/news-releases/building-out-advanced-packaging-portfolio-jcet-delivers-steady-revenue-growth-and-improved-profitability-in-q3-ytd-2026-302917052.html">JCET</a> (up 13%), <a href="https://investors.maxlinear.com/press-releases/detail/629/maxlinear-inc-announces-third-quarter-2026-financial">MaxLinear</a> (up 72%), <a href="https://www.nordicsemi.com/-/media/Investor-Relations-and-QA/Quarterly-Presentations/2026/NOD-Q3-2026_Presentation.pdf">Nordic</a> (up 32%), and <a href="https://www.ti.com/about-ti/newsroom/news-releases/2026/2026-10-21-ti-reports-third-quarter-2026-financial-results-and-shareholder-returns.html">TI</a> (up 28%).</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>By the numbers</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li>Global <a href="https://www.semi.org/en/semi-press-release/semi-forecasts-11.8-percent-growth-in-silicon-wafer-shipments-in-2026-with-record-highs-expected-through-2029">wafer shipments</a> are forecast to grow almost 12% in 2026, per <strong>SEMI</strong>.</li>
<li><a href="https://www.trendforce.com/presscenter/news/20261022-13279.html">Server CPU shipments</a> are expected to grow more than 40% in 2027, per <strong>TrendForce.</strong></li>
<li><strong>ESD Alliance </strong>reported Q2 <a href="https://www.semi.org/en/semi-press-release/electronic-system-design-industry-posts-%245.7-billion-in-revenue-in-q2-2026-esd-alliance-reports">electronic system design revenue rose</a> ~12% YoY.</li>
<li><a href="https://counterpointresearch.com/en/insights/global-pc-shipments-plunge-21-percent-in-q3-2026">Q3 global PC shipments fell 21%</a> YoY, as rising memory and component costs pushed up PC prices and led consumers to delay upgrades, per <strong>Counterpoint.</strong></li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Around the Valley: Oktobertech</strong></h3>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" decoding="async" class="alignnone wp-image-24283226" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-22-at-2.48.44-PM.png?resize=690%2C550&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="690" height="550" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-22-at-2.48.44-PM.png?resize=300%2C239&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-22-at-2.48.44-PM.png?resize=600%2C478&amp;ssl=1 600w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-22-at-2.48.44-PM.png?w=696&amp;ssl=1 696w" sizes="(max-width: 690px) 100vw, 690px" /><br />

<h2 id="Research"><strong>Research</strong></h2>
<p><strong>Northwestern University</strong>-led researchers demonstrated current-induced switching in <a href="https://www.mccormick.northwestern.edu/news/articles/2026/10/scientists-discover-new-spin-transfer-mechanism-in-antiferromagnets/">antiferromagnetic tunnel junctions</a> using octupole-driven spin-transfer torque. The nanoscale devices achieved 363% tunnel magnetoresistance at room temperature, pointing to a potential approach for nonvolatile antiferromagnetic memory.</p>
<p><strong>Institute for Basic Science</strong> and <strong>POSTECH</strong> researchers developed <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aei2693">2D transistors through selective conversion of WSe₂</a> into WTe₂ contacts, WS₂ semiconductor regions, and WOₓ insulating layers. The technique enabled integrated transistors and complementary logic without separately assembling different 2D materials.</p>
<p><strong>UC Berkeley</strong>,<strong> Samsung Electronics</strong>, and<strong> Intel</strong> researchers introduced a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1109/JXCDC.2026.3717204">nanoelectromechanically gated gain-cell architecture for embedded DRAM</a> to address limited data retention, parasitic coupling, and the need for boosted write voltages in conventional gain-cell designs. The approach explores an alternative embedded-memory architecture as SRAM scaling slows.</p>
<p data-pm-slice="1 1 []"><strong>University at Albany</strong> and other researchers designed and demonstrated a <a href="https://www.albany.edu/news-center/news/2026-ualbany-led-research-team-achieves-rare-milestone-ultra-high-voltage-power">15-kV silicon carbide insulated-gate bipolar transistor</a>, becoming the first U.S. academic institution to demonstrate this class of ultra-high-voltage device. A single switch could replace multiple lower-voltage devices in high-power systems, potentially reducing circuit complexity, equipment size, and energy losses.</p>

<h2 id="Security"><strong>Security</strong></h2>
<h3><strong>New offerings</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>Infineon</strong> expanded its PSOC Control family with <a href="https://www.infineon.com/technology-news/2026/inftn202610-009">PSC3M/P6 microcontrollers</a> for multi-motor control and power conversion, featuring post-quantum firmware security capabilities.</li>
<li><strong>Nvidia</strong> introduced <a href="https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/confidential-computing-model-builders-infrastructure/">Confidential Bare Metal</a>, extending confidential computing across Grace Blackwell and Rubin systems.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Alerts of the week</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li>Two critical vulnerabilities were discovered in the widely used open-source programming language PHP. The flaws could allow <a href="https://www.nsa.gov/press-room/press-releases-statements/press-release-view/article/4630238/nsa-advisory-critical-patches-recommended-for-php-vulnerabilities/">attackers to take control</a> of affected web servers.</li>
<li><strong>OpenAI</strong> disclosed that two internal AI agents <a href="https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/suppressing-misalignment-monitoring-alerts-and-disabling-misalignment-monitoring/">weakened misalignment monitoring</a> while performing coding tasks, including suppressing alerts to its security team and removing a monitoring integration.</li>
<li><strong>Siemens</strong> confirmed <a href="https://productcert.siemens.com/news/2026/10/19/active-exploitation-of-cve-2026-110936-in-siemens-software-center/">active exploitation of a vulnerability</a> in Siemens Software Center, in which attackers paired a genuine signed copy of the software with malicious DLL files that were loaded at startup. Siemens said its systems, products, and update channels were not breached and issued a fix.</li>
<li><strong>OpenCode</strong> reported a breach related to a <a href="https://x.com/opencode/status/2111519637049319818">large-scale distillation attack</a> affecting 1.4% of OpenCode Console users. Third-party OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google API keys stored by affected users may have been exposed.</li>
<li><strong>CISA</strong>’s alerts for the week are <a href="https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories">here</a>.</li>
</ul>
<h3><strong>Guidance</strong></h3>
<ul>
<li><strong>NIST</strong>,<strong> NSA</strong>, and <strong>CISA</strong> published <a href="https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/10/key-practices-incident-readiness-and-response-super-intelligence-training">10 voluntary practices</a> for responding to incidents during super-intelligence training and evaluation, including cases where agents take significant uninstructed actions that compromise security controls or human oversight.</li>
<li><strong>DHS</strong> ordered federal civilian agencies to <a href="https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-10-20/html/2026-21447.htm">stop procuring and remove DeepSeek</a> products, including products from affiliated entities and third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations.</li>
<li><strong>Institute for AI Policy and Strategy</strong> says <a href="https://www.iaps.ai/research/honeypots-for-ai-agent-insider-threats">honeypots could help detect insider threats from AI agents</a> by using decoy credentials, servers and other traps to flag unauthorized actions. Detection has the strongest evidence base, though honeypots only cover paths where defenders deploy them.</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="Trending Video"><strong>Trending Video</strong></h2>
<p><a href="https://semiengineering.com/scaling-data-movement-for-physical-ai/">Scaling Data Movement For Physical AI</a>: Physical AI poses a host of new challenges for chip engineers. These systems contain a mix of compute elements, which collectively must process a stream of real-time data, analyze it, make decisions, and still function long enough on a battery to be useful. The key here is deciding what data gets processed where, and how to minimize the movement of data.</p>
<p><iframe src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/tt5Xcjf9MVo" width="480" height="270" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen="allowfullscreen" data-mce-fragment="1"></iframe></p>

<h2 id="Quantum Hardware"><strong>Quantum Hardware</strong></h2>
<p><strong>Quantinuum</strong> reported <a href="https://www.quantinuum.com/press-releases/quantinuum-breaks-error-correction-world-record-by-10x-validating-its-leading-path-to-fault-tolerant-quantum-computing-by-2029">99.9995% logical memory fidelity</a> per error-correction cycle on its Helios trapped-ion system using a distance-7 color code.</p>
<p><strong>Alice &amp; Bob</strong> built and operated <a href="https://alice-bob.com/newsroom/alice-bob-results/">three cat-qubit demonstrators</a> — two using 6-qubit chips and one using a 12-qubit chip — demonstrating noise-biased CNOT gates, repeated error-correction cycles, and a non-Clifford gate. Its measured logical error rate has not yet fallen below the error-correction threshold.</p>
<p><strong>UW</strong> and <strong>PNNL</strong> researchers developed a hybrid gallium-phosphide-on-diamond photonic platform for <a href="https://www.optica.org/about/newsroom/news_releases/2026/hybrid_gap-on-diamond_platform_strengthens_quantum-light_interactions">coupling photons to silicon-vacancy qubits</a>. They fabricated more than 600 nanophotonic cavities with a 99.5% yield and demonstrated single-shot electron-spin readout.</p>
<p data-pm-slice="1 1 []"><strong>DGIST</strong>,<strong> Tokyo University of Science</strong>,<strong> RIKEN</strong>, et al., demonstrated a <a href="https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-78631-5">protected cat-qutrit manifold</a> using a three-photon Kerr parametric oscillator. The team observed three-photon Rabi oscillations, three-component cat states and an energy gap separating the qutrit manifold from excited states.</p>
<p data-pm-slice="1 1 []"><strong>McKinsey</strong> says scaling <a href="https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/tech-and-ai/our-insights/three-horizons-of-quantum-a-business-road-map-to-the-future-computing-economy">fault-tolerant quantum hardware</a> is becoming a manufacturing challenge, requiring major expansion in lasers, cryogenics, control electronics and fabrication capacity. The firm also noted that no single qubit technology has yet emerged as the clear winner.</p>
<hr />
<h2 id="Workforce, Education"><strong>Workforce, Education</strong></h2>
<p><strong>Qualcomm</strong> will begin notifying employees in November about <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/qualcomm-cut-jobs-worldwide-performance-focused-layoffs-internal-memo-shows-2026-10-20/">global job cuts</a> following its annual performance reviews, reports Reuters, but the company has not disclosed how many positions will be affected.</p>
<p><strong>Micron</strong> will introduce <a href="https://www.cna.com.tw/news/afe/202610220264.aspx">quarterly profit-linked bonuses</a> for employees worldwide beginning in fiscal 2027, following an agreement with its Taichung union in <strong>Taiwan.</strong> The company also plans salary adjustments, increased retirement contributions and additional paid leave for Taiwan employees.</p>
<p><strong>Hoover Institution</strong> senior fellow Paola Sapienza argues that tighter U.S. <a href="https://www.hoover.org/research/america-closing-door-talent">high-skilled immigration policies</a>, including new H-1B restrictions and proposed limits on student visas, could make it harder for the chip industry to recruit specialized engineers and researchers as countries including the UK step up efforts to attract technical talent.</p>
<p><strong>Malaysia</strong> said <a href="https://web26.bernama.com/radio/news.php?id=2623411">22,849 people have been trained for the semiconductor sector</a> through the third quarter of 2026, toward its goal of developing 60,000 highly skilled semiconductor engineers by 2030. Training covers IC design, advanced packaging, wafer fabrication, embedded systems and automation, while the government is establishing a semiconductor academy in Penang focused on IC design, fabrication and advanced packaging.</p>

		<title>Beyond The EPE Budget: Building The Next Generation Of Computational Lithography</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/beyond-the-epe-budget-building-the-next-generation-of-computational-lithography/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/beyond-the-epe-budget-building-the-next-generation-of-computational-lithography/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Germain Fenger]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 22 Oct 2026 07:08:02 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - MD]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Manufacturing Solutions]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Manufacturing, Packaging and Materials]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[computational lithography]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[EDA]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[edge placement error]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[EPE]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[lithography]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[metrology]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[OPC]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[optical proximity correction]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Synopsys]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24283024</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Why better models, richer metrology, explainable AI, and cross-industry collaboration must come together to extend semiconductor scaling.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/beyond-the-epe-budget-building-the-next-generation-of-computational-lithography/">Beyond The EPE Budget: Building The Next Generation Of Computational Lithography</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>At the recent SPIE Photomask Technology + Extreme Ultraviolet Lithography conference, an expert panel discussed the growing importance of edge placement error (EPE). I had the pleasure of joining moderator Jed Rankin of IBM and fellow panelists Hans Stiepan of Carl Zeiss SMT, Ezequiel Vidal-Russell of Micron Technology, Jo Finders of ASML, Il-Yong Jang of Tekscend, and Vivek Balasubramanian of Applied Materials. Together, we brought perspectives spanning OPC and EDA, mask technology, lithography systems, materials, and metrology. One point quickly became clear: EPE is no longer a narrow lithography metric. It is becoming a system-level measure of how well our industry can translate design intent into a manufacturable, high-yielding device. The mask, scanner, resist, etch process, metrology, OPC, and downstream integration all contribute. Each discipline can optimize its own part, but a collection of local optima does not automatically produce the best device—even if everyone arrives with an excellent slide explaining why their part is already optimized.</p>
<h2>EPE has become a system problem</h2>
<p>As pitch scaling becomes more difficult, tighter control of placement, variability, and pattern fidelity becomes one of the main paths to continued scaling. The challenge is that EPE is an unbounded budget. Mask three-dimensional effects, absorber profile, sidewall angle, critical-dimension uniformity, registration, scanner behavior, resist variability, etch, stochastic effects, process-induced stress, and even wafer or die bonding can all move an edge or change its electrical consequence. Yet the audience survey delivered a wonderfully familiar verdict: OPC was viewed both as a major source of EPE and as the leading place from which future EPE reduction would come. In other words, OPC was cast as both the villain and the superhero. Jed leaned into the joke, asking what Ezequiel and I would need from the rest of the industry to carry that superhero burden. By the final poll, confidence in OPC had risen to 58 percent—prompting the prediction that I might appear next time in tights. I am happy to accept the confidence; the cape may be negotiable.</p>
<h2>The EDA challenge: Stop treating residual error as one big bucket</h2>
<p>Today, many effects that are difficult to isolate are absorbed into empirical corrections, rule tables, or an “etch” term. This is pragmatic and often necessary in production, where repeatability, runtime, yield, and schedule outweigh a perfect explanation. Ezequiel captured the dilemma well: after seeing the poll, he was not sure whether the OPC community should feel encouraged or concerned. The audience clearly expected OPC to take care of every systematic and correctable effect—and, where possible, reduce sensitivity to the uncorrectable ones too. That is an impressive job description for any superhero. But even OPC needs good physics, good data, and a process window; it cannot leap an inaccurate model in a single bound. As tolerances shrink, the effects we sweep into the correction bucket become large relative to the remaining process window. EDA must therefore represent the real manufacturing system more completely: not an idealized mask with uniform properties, but pattern-dependent mask profiles, realistic metrology behavior, scanner effects, process variability, and the interactions among them.</p>
<h2>Not more data, better data</h2>
<h2></h2>
<p>More data alone is not the answer. We need data that is physically meaningful, sufficiently repeatable for manufacturing, and connected to the patterns that matter on the wafer. A single SEM image contains far more information than one extracted CD. Contours, profiles, roughness, placement, local geometry, and pattern context can all inform better models. At the same time, no fab can measure everything. OPC and process models should help identify the patterns with the highest wafer sensitivity, rank the hotspots, and translate that sensitivity into mask and wafer metrology requirements. This closes a critical loop: modeling guides measurement, measurement improves modeling, and both focus resources on yield-relevant problems.</p>
<h2>AI must be paired with physics and validation</h2>
<p>I believe artificial intelligence will deliver one of the largest future gains in EPE reduction. Machine learning can capture residual systematic behavior that is difficult to model directly, while agentic systems can coordinate optimization across traditionally separate domains. But semiconductor manufacturing cannot rely on an unexplained black box. A model that reports zero EPE without showing why it is trustworthy is not production-ready. The path forward is explainable AI anchored by rigorous simulation, validated against appropriate metrology, bounded by known physics, and monitored for the conditions in which it can safely be applied.</p>
<h2>Agentic systems should solve defined engineering problems</h2>
<p>Agentic AI should not be turned loose across the ecosystem with the assumption that it will discover a global optimum on its own. Adoption will begin with well-defined problems: reducing global CDU, selecting robust mask geometries, optimizing source and mask together, prioritizing metrology, or connecting pattern variation to electrical impact. For each problem, we must define the objective, the data required, the knobs the system may turn, the physical constraints, and the validation criteria. Confidence will grow locally, and successful agents can then be connected into broader workflows.</p>
<h2>EDA must connect EPE to power, performance, area, cost, and yield</h2>
<p>Our customers do not sell EPE; they sell products defined by power, performance, area, cost, and yield. Some EPE limits are hard geometric boundaries: exceed them and a structure shorts, opens, or fails. Other errors occupy a gray zone where their importance depends on device behavior. EDA has an opportunity to bridge that gap by bringing electrical simulation, stochastic analysis, lithography, mask optimization, process modeling, and design technology co-optimization into a common decision flow. The goal is not simply the smallest geometric error everywhere. It is the right allocation of process margin where it creates the greatest product value.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone wp-image-24283025 size-full" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Synopsys_Beyond-the-EPE-Budget-fig1.webp?resize=1335%2C621&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="1335" height="621" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Synopsys_Beyond-the-EPE-Budget-fig1.webp?w=1335&amp;ssl=1 1335w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Synopsys_Beyond-the-EPE-Budget-fig1.webp?resize=300%2C140&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Synopsys_Beyond-the-EPE-Budget-fig1.webp?resize=1024%2C476&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Synopsys_Beyond-the-EPE-Budget-fig1.webp?resize=768%2C357&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Synopsys_Beyond-the-EPE-Budget-fig1.webp?resize=600%2C279&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /></p>
<p><strong>Fig. 1: Process simulations using stochastic modeling techniques can predict process characteristics that lead to electrical problems with a design before reticles are built.</strong></p>
<h2>Collaboration is the path from local to global optimization</h2>
<p>Foundries and IDMs sit at the center of this opportunity because they see the complete manufacturing flow and hold the data that connects mask, scanner, process, device, and yield. EDA providers need deeper partnerships with them, as well as with mask makers, metrology suppliers, and lithography equipment providers. Those partnerships must enable secure, purposeful sharing of data and context—not data collection for its own sake. The highest-value collaboration will define common EPE frameworks, expose the relevant process sensitivities, prioritize the dominant contributors, and establish closed feedback loops at the stage where each error can still be understood and corrected.</p>
<h2>A practical direction for the industry</h2>
<ul>
<li><strong>Build fuller physical representations.</strong> Model pattern-dependent mask structure, process interactions, stochastic behavior, and time-dependent change rather than hiding them in a single residual term.</li>
<li><strong>Make metrology model-driven and device-relevant.</strong> Use OPC and simulation to identify sensitive patterns, then measure the locations and attributes that most strongly affect wafer performance.</li>
<li><strong>Combine AI with rigorous simulation.</strong> Use machine learning to capture residuals and accelerate prediction, while physics-based models provide explainability, boundaries, and validation.</li>
<li><strong>Apply agentic systems to bounded problems first.</strong> Define the target, inputs, controls, and success criteria before expanding across workflows.</li>
<li><strong>Optimize for product outcomes.</strong> Connect EPE decisions to power, performance, area, cost, yield, and manufacturability.</li>
<li><strong>Close loops across the ecosystem.</strong> Align EDA, mask, metrology, scanner, foundry, and IDM teams around common definitions and prioritized contributors.</li>
</ul>
<h2>The EPE era will last for decades</h2>
<p>EPE scaling is not a temporary phase. As the industry moves from planar scaling to three-dimensional integration and eventually to time-dependent, system-level optimization, the definition of EPE will continue to evolve. Wafer-to-die bonding, new device architectures, curvilinear masks, high-NA lithography, and tighter coupling between manufacturing and electrical performance will create new correction and optimization problems. The opportunity for EDA is to become the connective intelligence across these domains—combining physics, data, and purposeful AI to turn fragmented process knowledge into manufacturable outcomes. The audience may be ready to call OPC the savior of EPE, and I appreciate the vote of confidence. But the real superpower will come from giving OPC better mask knowledge, better metrology, better process context, and tighter links to device performance. That is how we extend scaling: not by asking one team to wear the cape, but by enabling every part of the ecosystem to work together.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/beyond-the-epe-budget-building-the-next-generation-of-computational-lithography/">Beyond The EPE Budget: Building The Next Generation Of Computational Lithography</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>

		<title>PVTW: Extending Silicon Characterization From PVT To Real-World Workload</title>
		<link>https://semiengineering.com/pvtw-extending-silicon-characterization-from-pvt-to-real-world-workload/</link>
					<comments>https://semiengineering.com/pvtw-extending-silicon-characterization-from-pvt-to-real-world-workload/#respond</comments>
		
		<dc:creator><![CDATA[Gerard John]]></dc:creator>
		<pubDate>Thu, 22 Oct 2026 07:07:27 +0000</pubDate>
				<category><![CDATA[Blogs - MD]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Chip, Package, System]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Manufacturing, Packaging and Materials]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[Amkor]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[ATE]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[characterization]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[PVT]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[PVTW]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[SLT]]></category>
		<category><![CDATA[system-level test]]></category>
		<guid isPermaLink="false">https://semiengineering.com/?p=24283098</guid>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>Two devices operating at exactly the same voltage, frequency, and temperature can behave differently depending on what they are being asked to do.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/pvtw-extending-silicon-characterization-from-pvt-to-real-world-workload/">PVTW: Extending Silicon Characterization From PVT To Real-World Workload</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p>For decades, silicon characterization has been built around Process, Voltage, and Temperature, or PVT. We characterize devices across process variation, sweep voltage and frequency, control temperature, generate SHMOO plots, and establish the operating envelope of the silicon.</p>
<p>That methodology remains fundamental. But today&#8217;s high-performance processors are increasingly systems in their own right. An AI accelerator may contain thousands of compute elements, distributed SRAM, high-speed SerDes, PCIe and Ethernet interfaces, multiple clock and power domains, advanced packaging, firmware, operating systems, compilers and application software.</p>
<p>Two devices operating at exactly the same voltage, frequency, and temperature can behave differently depending on what they are being asked to do.</p>
<p>This suggests adding another dimension: <strong>PVTW: Process × Voltage × Temperature × Workload</strong></p>
<p>Frequency can be swept within this characterization space to determine operating margin.</p>
<p>The objective is not to replace traditional ATE characterization with System Level Test. It is to combine the electrical precision and control available from ATE with the realistic operating environment available from SLT, while retaining the ability to use either independently.</p>
<h2>One platform, two capabilities, three modes</h2>
<p>One way to implement PVTW is through a hybrid characterization architecture integrating ATE resources and SLT capability.</p>
<p>There is no reason to recreate resources that already exist in ATE. Existing ATE infrastructure, including older generation platforms, can provide programmable device power supplies, individual rail control and measurement, variable frequency clocks, digital stimulus and capture, ATPG and structural content, parametric measurements, and conventional SHMOO characterization.</p>
<p>SLT provides something fundamentally different: the application environment.</p>
<p>The processor can boot firmware and an operating system, load drivers and runtime software, and execute deterministic workloads designed to exercise specific parts of the architecture. For an AI processor, those workloads might emphasize compute, SRAM, external memory, PCIe, Ethernet, or chip-to-chip communication. Other workloads could intentionally activate several simultaneously to create realistic system stress.</p>
<p>The architecture therefore provides three modes. ATE mode performs conventional electrical, structural, and parametric characterization. SLT mode executes controlled system workloads. Combined mode uses ATE resources to control and measure electrical conditions while the device executes an SLT workload.</p>
<p>Combined mode is where PVTW becomes particularly interesting.</p>
<h2>From conventional SHMOO to workload SHMOO</h2>
<p>Consider a conventional voltage and frequency SHMOO using ATPG or appropriate functional content. At a controlled temperature, establish the operating boundary.</p>
<p>Now boot the processor, establish a deterministic workload, and repeat the sweep.</p>
<p>Start with a compute-intensive workload. Repeat with SRAM, external memory, PCIe, and Ethernet-intensive workloads. Finally, create combinations that deliberately generate simultaneous compute, memory, and I/O activity.</p>
<p>Suppose an ATPG SHMOO indicates that a device operates correctly down to 0.72 V at a particular frequency, while an SRAM-intensive application begins producing errors at 0.76 V.</p>
<p>That 40 mV difference is not simply a disagreement between ATE and SLT. It is characterization information.</p>
<p>Something about the workload is consuming margin. Is it SRAM timing? Clock distribution? IR drop? Simultaneous switching noise? A thermal gradient? Power delivery? Or an interaction among several subsystems?</p>
<h2>Characterization requires control</h2>
<p>There is an important distinction between testing and characterization.</p>
<p>Booting Linux, running an AI workload, and observing whether the processor crashes is useful testing. Characterization requires controlled variables, repeatability, and the ability to deliberately move the operating boundary.</p>
<p>Hold workload, temperature, and frequency constant while sweeping a selected voltage rail. Then hold workload, temperature, and voltage constant while sweeping frequency. Change temperature and repeat.</p>
<p>The hybrid architecture can go deeper. Hold I/O and memory rails constant while margining the core rail during a compute workload. Then margin a memory-related rail while executing a memory-intensive workload.</p>
<p>We can begin creating subsystem-specific workload SHMOOs that connect:</p>
<ul>
<li>Workload → Subsystem → Electrical Margin</li>
</ul>
<h2>From workload failure to electrical debug</h2>
<p>Consider a device that passes Wafer Sort and Final Test but develops errors after a sustained application workload. Cooling reduces the failure rate, while increasing the core voltage does not eliminate the problem. Telemetry indicates that most errors are associated with the same memory interface or byte lane, although the failing addresses move.</p>
<p>The device does not necessarily have to leave the characterization platform.</p>
<p>SLT mode can expose the system behavior and help isolate the subsystem. The platform can operate in ATE mode to investigate electrical and structural characteristics using programmable power, clock control, ATPG, functional patterns, and parametric measurements.</p>
<p>Or both capabilities can operate together. The workload can reproduce the marginal condition while ATE resources manipulate selected rails and clocks.</p>
<p>The three modes therefore answer different questions. SLT exposes the behavior. ATE investigates the electrical and structural characteristics. Combined mode characterizes their interaction.</p>
<p>This creates a tight engineering loop:</p>
<p>Create workload → Observe marginality → Isolate subsystem → Characterize electrically → Modify conditions → Repeat workload → Establish correlation → Determine root cause</p>
<p>For me, that is the interesting possibility behind PVTW. SLT no longer needs to be viewed only as a downstream production screen. Combined intelligently with ATE resources, it can become part of a controlled silicon characterization environment.</p>
<p>But this leads to another question. If two devices both PASS, are they actually equivalent?</p>
<p>That is the subject of Part 2: Beyond Pass/Fail: Characterizing Silicon Margin with PVTW.</p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/pvtw-extending-silicon-characterization-from-pvt-to-real-world-workload/">PVTW: Extending Silicon Characterization From PVT To Real-World Workload</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></content:encoded>

					<description><![CDATA[<p>SEMICON West 2026: Advanced packaging, photonics, test, and AI are increasingly intertwined; very different conversations ahead. </p>
<p>The post <a href="https://semiengineering.com/chip-scaling-moves-beyond-the-transistor/">Chip Scaling Moves Beyond The Transistor</a> appeared first on <a href="https://semiengineering.com">Semiconductor Engineering</a>.</p>
]]></description>
										<content:encoded><![CDATA[<p><strong>Key Takeaways:</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>The semiconductor industry reached $1 trillion years early, but keeping pace with demand now depends on systems integration as much as transistor scaling.</li>
<li>Packaging, photonics, power, and test are converging into one optimization problem, which means improving any one of them can move the bottleneck somewhere else.</li>
<li>AI is shifting from the workload the industry serves to a tool it uses, and the open question is how much engineering and manufacturing authority it will be given.</li>
</ul>
<hr />
<p>When SEMICON West gathered in San Francisco in 2023, the semiconductor industry was forecasting a path to $1 trillion in annual revenue by 2030. Three years later, the industry has already blown past that number. SEMICON West 2026 returned to San Francisco with a sold-out exhibit floor, more than 30,000 attendees, and an industry confronting a different question: How does it keep up with the growth it once aimed for?</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="wp-image-24283033 alignleft" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-9.55.38-AM.png?resize=212%2C165&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="212" height="165" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-9.55.38-AM.png?w=1739&amp;ssl=1 1739w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-9.55.38-AM.png?resize=300%2C233&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-9.55.38-AM.png?resize=1024%2C796&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-9.55.38-AM.png?resize=768%2C597&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-9.55.38-AM.png?resize=1536%2C1193&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-9.55.38-AM.png?resize=600%2C466&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 212px) 100vw, 212px" /> SEMI&#8217;s own projections show how steep that curve has become. In his opening keynote, SEMI President and CEO Ajit Manocha forecast a market of more than $2 trillion by 2030, and potentially $3 trillion by 2035. At the SEMI Market Symposium, the association projected 300mm fab equipment spending of $149 billion this year, rising to $227 billion by 2029, with construction beginning on 20 new 300mm fabs or production lines in 2026 alone.</p>
<p>AI infrastructure is driving much of that growth, but electrification, autonomous vehicles, robotics, and industrial automation are adding semiconductor content, as well. What makes the current expansion unusual is the growing complexity of the systems those chips will enable, not the almost insatiable demand for chips.</p>
<p>“We’ve started talking about how to re-engineer engineering because you need to co-design and optimize across multiple intersections,” said Sassine Ghazi, president and CEO of <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/synopsys-inc/">Synopsys</a>. “That’s at the physics level, material, process technology, architecture, design, along with the software and the model itself, because the model itself is what’s defining the workload, and how do you optimize along that stack?”</p>
<p>Across presentations, panels, and discussions on the show floor, several issues kept converging around that problem. Advanced packaging is becoming part of system architecture. Photonics is moving closer to compute, while bringing new manufacturing and test challenges with it. Test, inspection and metrology have to follow more complicated assemblies and manufacturing histories. And AI is moving from something the industry builds to something it uses to design and manufacture. None of these technologies is new, but each is becoming harder to optimize independently, and that may be the clearest indication of what the industry will be working on in the coming years.</p>
<p><strong>Scaling becomes a system-level challenge </strong><br />
The shift was apparent in conversations ranging from transistor scaling and HBM to advanced packaging, optical interconnects, and cooling, where improving any one of those can move a bottleneck elsewhere. More compute increases pressure on memory bandwidth and power delivery. Moving memory closer reduces data movement but concentrates heat. Disaggregating a large die can improve yield and allow functions to use different process nodes, but it creates more interfaces that have to be connected, powered, cooled, and tested.</p>
<p>“Packaging is no longer simply the place where semiconductor innovation ends,” said Lalitha Immaneni, vice president of semiconductor R&amp;D at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/intel-foundry/">Intel Foundry</a>. “Increasingly, it’s the place where system innovation begins.”</p>
<p>That makes memory, data movement, power delivery, and thermal management part of the architecture rather than downstream considerations.</p>
<p>“The challenge is not to co-optimize one component,” Immaneni said. “It is to co-optimize across the system from end to end between silicon, packaging, and platform.”</p>
<p>Nitin Deshpande, Marvell&#8217;s vice president of advanced packaging, made a similar point during imec’s pre-show ITF USA program. “The package is really becoming a system where the compute, the memory, the interconnects, the power, the cooling, all of these things come together.”</p>
<p>Making those pieces work together is only part of the challenge. Larger, more heterogeneous packages still have to become high-volume products with acceptable yield, reliability, and cost.</p>
<p>“We can have very cool concepts, but if we cannot scale these into high volumes, if we cannot have a high-yielding, reliable process with a supply chain that can provide the parts in time, everything that we do cannot be converted into a business,” Deshpande said.</p>
<p>Patrick Vandenameele, CEO of imec, noted that AI infrastructure can keep growing by adding accelerators and racks, but adding hardware isn’t scaling in the traditional semiconductor sense. “These data centers are true engineering marvels,” he said. “But at the same time, this is not what we semiconductor people call scaling. It looks a little bit more like multiplication.”</p>
<p>That distinction helps explain why so many separate topics at SEMICON West kept leading back to the same place. The industry isn’t abandoning transistor scaling. It’s adding another level above it, where performance depends on how effectively different technologies can be combined into a functional system.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24283035" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-9.45.13-AM-scaled.png?resize=2560%2C1452&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="2560" height="1452" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-9.45.13-AM-scaled.png?w=2560&amp;ssl=1 2560w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-9.45.13-AM-scaled.png?resize=300%2C170&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-9.45.13-AM-scaled.png?resize=1024%2C581&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-9.45.13-AM-scaled.png?resize=768%2C435&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-9.45.13-AM-scaled.png?resize=1536%2C871&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-9.45.13-AM-scaled.png?resize=2048%2C1161&amp;ssl=1 2048w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-9.45.13-AM-scaled.png?resize=600%2C340&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><br />
<strong>Fig. 2: Redefining a system. Source: SEMI</strong></p>
<p><strong>AI moves from assistant to operator </strong><br />
AI was nearly impossible to avoid at SEMICON West, but the conversation is shifting. Machine learning has been part of design, process control, and defect classification for years, and generative AI added natural-language access to complicated tools and data. Agentic AI goes further, allowing engineers to hand an agent an objective and let it invoke other tools, models, or agents to reach it.</p>
<p>“We started from an assistant copilot to generative capability to now what we’re describing as long-horizon autonomous agents, where instead of giving a prompt, you give an outcome,” said Synopsys’ Ghazi.</p>
<p>The appeal of agentic AI becomes clearer when looking at the size of the spaces engineers are being asked to optimize. “The space that we’re optimizing in has exploded,” said David Fried, chief AI officer and corporate vice president of Semiverse Solutions at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/lam-research/">Lam Research</a>. “We’ve now gotten to a place where the parameter set is intractable.”</p>
<p>A current Lam etcher, for example, can have a potential recipe space on the order of 10<sup>23</sup> possibilities, which is well beyond what any engineer can explore manually. “That’s really where AI is coming to the rescue,” Fried said. “It’s the ability to get through massive multi-parameter dimensional spaces, massive sets of intertwined sensitivities between a much larger parameter space, and a much larger spec space.”</p>
<p>Acting on what AI finds is where the discussion gets more complicated. Flagging an unusual process signature is different from letting an AI system alter a recipe, and predicting equipment degradation is different from stopping production. Ghazi said Synopsys already has engagements where autonomous agents can take a customer specification through verified RTL. This is work that traditionally required multiple engineers and months. Human judgment is still needed to define the architecture and sign off before manufacturing, but the boundary is moving.</p>
<p>On the manufacturing side, that raises questions likely to become more prominent over the next year. What decisions can an agent make without approval? How much of its constraint comes from physics-based models rather than statistical inference? What evidence is required before an autonomous decision can affect production?</p>
<p>The question coming out of SEMICON West isn’t whether AI will be used to design and manufacture semiconductors. That&#8217;s already happening. The new question is how much authority engineers are prepared to give it.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="alignnone size-full wp-image-24283036" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-11.04.44-AM-scaled.png?resize=2560%2C1149&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="2560" height="1149" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-11.04.44-AM-scaled.png?w=2560&amp;ssl=1 2560w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-11.04.44-AM-scaled.png?resize=300%2C135&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-11.04.44-AM-scaled.png?resize=1024%2C460&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-11.04.44-AM-scaled.png?resize=768%2C345&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-11.04.44-AM-scaled.png?resize=1536%2C689&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-11.04.44-AM-scaled.png?resize=2048%2C919&amp;ssl=1 2048w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-11.04.44-AM-scaled.png?resize=600%2C269&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><br />
<strong>Fig. 3: What comes next is an evolving topic of great interest to a lot of people. Source: SEMI</strong></p>
<p><strong>Packaging has to become manufacturable </strong><br />
Advanced packaging showed up almost everywhere, but the emphasis has moved beyond proving that heterogeneous integration works. The harder problem is doing it repeatedly, economically, and at volume while protecting the value accumulated during assembly. That is changing the meaning of “known good.”</p>
<p>Known-good die has been an objective for years, because attaching a bad die to a good package wastes everything around it. As substrates, bridges, and intermediate assemblies grow more complicated and expensive, the same logic is moving outward.</p>
<p>“Even though the bridge is a passive component with just metal lines, we sort it,” said Ravi Mahajan, Intel fellow and director of substrate and advanced packaging pathfinding at Intel Foundry<strong>.</strong> “We make sure we have known-good bridges going into a package, and what comes out should be a known-good package.”</p>
<p>Mahajan was careful to treat “known good” as an aspiration rather than an absolute.</p>
<p>“You bring into your assembly process a known-good substrate, and the word ‘known-good’ has to be understood,” Mahajan said. “It’s not always known-good, but you know as much of this as you can. And to do that, you put in the right kind of features to test so that you have as much coverage as possible.”</p>
<p>ASE is approaching the problem in much the same way. In some fan-out flows, the interconnect structure can be fully tested before any active silicon is attached.</p>
<p>“The known-good methodology is what we’re striving for,” said Yin Chang, executive vice president of <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/ase/">ASE</a>. “Everything we do, every layer, we have the ability to confirm that it is good before we put on the most expensive part.”</p>
<p>Some silicon and HBM combinations can represent as much as $30,000 in value, and ASE uses AOI and X-ray extensively, with AI helping distinguish subtle differences across assemblies that can contain as many as half a million joints.</p>
<p>“The goal for our industry is trying to take out as much unknown as we can in the overall processes,” Chang said. “It is too expensive already today. We just can’t scrap anything.”</p>
<p>Assembly complicates that goal. Bonding creates interfaces that didn’t exist when the individual components were inspected, and heat, pressure, and materials interactions can alter the state of the assembly, so some defects can’t be detected until another process step has occurred. The objective progressively becomes how to reduce uncertainty as value is added, and the sampling calculation shifts from how much inspection maintains yield to how much uncertainty a manufacturer can afford to carry into the next step.</p>
<p><strong>Test follows the system </strong><br />
That same pressure is reshaping test, particularly as photonics enters the package. Digital manufacturing test compares a response with an expected result, but optical devices can produce a range of acceptable responses that still have to be correlated with possible defects. Co-packaged optics adds a physical problem, as well.</p>
<p>“What our customers are demanding from OSATs is to be able to do dual-sided electrical/optical probe and expect efficiencies,” said Vineet Pancholi, senior director, manufacturing test technologist at <a href="https://semiengineering.com/entities/amkor-technology/">Amkor</a>. “Even if the ASPs are that high, they are still looking for manufacturing tests to be way more efficient.”</p>
<p>“The mechanical structure is different,” Pancholi said. “The package, physical x,y,z, weight of the package, the density of the package — that’s all changing. All of it is changing.” Asked whether those changes were increasing test-cell time, the number of insertions, or both, he added. &#8220;The high-level test workflow with probe, burn-in, final test, and system-level-test insertions remains the same. However, since the optical test content is newly being architected, test times are expected to be higher in the short term. They are expected to lower once defects based on fabrication and assembly process maturity are attained.”</p>
<p>Knowing where a problem occurred also depends increasingly on retaining information from earlier process steps.</p>
<p>“Even if you don’t know exactly which level it is, you can bracket the issue from historical images,&#8221; said Reiner Fenske, CEO of Microtronic.</p>
<p>Microtronic is approaching inspection partly as a historical record, retaining wafer images that can be compared across process steps when a defect appears later. That becomes increasingly valuable as additional layers make earlier defects difficult or impossible to see.</p>
<p>“The information that we gather is so valuable to them that throughput is a secondary issue, but having the history, that’s key,” Fenske said. “So six months from now, you can retrieve the entire lot run from archive which retains all of the data and images.”</p>
<p>Determining whether something is good increasingly requires context. Wafer test results, inspection data, assembly history and earlier insertions can be fed forward to alter later testing or fed backward to identify process drift. At the same time, following a die from its original wafer coordinates through reconstituted wafers, panels and multi-die assemblies makes traceability much harder.</p>
<p>Test is becoming less a final pass/fail gate than a continuous evidence trail, and that brings it into the AI discussion as well. AI can find patterns across that history, but only if the data can be tied to the right device, process step, and physical context.</p>
<p><strong>Photonics faces manufacturing challenges </strong><br />
The motivation for photonics is well established. Electrical interconnects struggle with power and signal integrity as bandwidth and distance rise, pushing optics from pluggable modules toward near-package and co-packaged designs. The closer optics gets to compute, however, the more the problem moves into semiconductor manufacturing.</p>
<p>“For precision bonding, it needs to not only control in all six degrees of freedom,” said Huan Ma, senior technologist at Intel Foundry. “It also needs to deliver throughput at a semiconductor manufacturing scale with automation and standardized material handling.”</p>
<p>The same requirement extends to materials, which have to preserve alignment through assembly, reflow and reliability stresses, and to metrology.</p>
<p>“For metrology and inspection, how do we measure the variables that actually predict optical yield?” Ma said. “We need to measure the geometry, the angles, the positions of optical features, and what really matters to the insertion loss and to the coupling efficiency. Co-packaged optics will not scale just because the optics work. It will only scale when we industrialize the optics through advanced packaging.”</p>
<p>The same issues surfaced across the show floor. EV Group pointed to the metrology and throughput burden of measuring multiple alignment points across hundreds of dies in die-to-wafer integration. Lam Research discussed waveguide fabrication, new modulator materials, and fiber coupling. Advantest described high-volume test as one of the remaining bottlenecks, with electro-optical probing and optical connectors adding requirements that don’t exist in electrical test.</p>
<p>Assembly complicates known-good here, too, because alignment, bonding, thermal processing and fiber attachment can alter an optical path that met specification before integration.</p>
<p>“Coming through the door, you have an understanding of what is known good on the PIC and the EIC,” Intel’s Mahajan said. “The biggest question is how do you ensure you have alignment? These processes in photonics are not recoverable and not reworkable, so we have spent a lot of time figuring out the yield limiters in assembly.”</p>
<p>Mahajan doesn’t see an intrinsic barrier, pointing to fiber attachment as a step considered particularly difficult less than a decade ago, but which has improved substantially through repeated process learning.</p>
<p>“I cannot think of any intrinsic showstoppers in any of these processes,” he said. “It’s now a matter of practice to do it right.”</p>
<p>The question surrounding co-packaged optics is becoming less about whether the technology can work and more about how quickly it can be aligned, inspected, tested, and manufactured at semiconductor volumes.</p>
<p><strong>Engineering boundaries are blurring </strong><br />
What stood out at SEMICON West was how often discussions in one area crossed into another. A package decision becomes a thermal decision. Memory placement becomes a power decision. Photonics becomes a packaging and test problem, inspection becomes a data problem, and manufacturing data becomes an AI problem. The old engineering boundaries still exist organizationally, but they increasingly don’t describe the physical system.</p>
<p>In her keynote, Intel’s Immaneni described the response as moving beyond design-technology co-optimization toward system-technology co-optimization, where silicon, packaging, and platform are considered together.</p>
<p>“A beautiful technology can be a good choice, but if I cannot manufacture it repeatedly, quickly, and with high quality, then it is not a customer technology,” she said.</p>
<p>Digital twins fit into the same transition, but their value depends on connecting electrical, thermal, mechanical, and manufacturing models closely enough that a decision in one domain can be evaluated against its consequences in the others. During his discussion with Semiconductor Engineering Editor-in-Chief Ed Sperling, Synopsys’ Ghazi added the workload to that list, since model behavior can drive power and thermal conditions in the hardware underneath it. As AI expands into robots, vehicles and other physical systems, sensors, safety requirements and real-time constraints compound the problem further.</p>
<p><strong>Conclusion: Five months to Phoenix </strong><br />
SEMICON West won’t have a full year to see how those conversations develop. This was the show’s last scheduled run in San Francisco. SEMI has signed a three-year agreement with Phoenix, and the next event moves to the Phoenix Convention Center March 30 through April 1, 2027, beginning a new spring schedule. That leaves about five months between shows, and some useful markers should be visible by then.</p>
<p><img data-recalc-dims="1" loading="lazy" decoding="async" class="aligncenter wp-image-24283034 size-full" src="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-9.54.18-AM-scaled.png?resize=2560%2C1413&#038;ssl=1" alt="" width="2560" height="1413" srcset="https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-9.54.18-AM-scaled.png?w=2560&amp;ssl=1 2560w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-9.54.18-AM-scaled.png?resize=300%2C166&amp;ssl=1 300w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-9.54.18-AM-scaled.png?resize=1024%2C565&amp;ssl=1 1024w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-9.54.18-AM-scaled.png?resize=768%2C424&amp;ssl=1 768w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-9.54.18-AM-scaled.png?resize=1536%2C848&amp;ssl=1 1536w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-9.54.18-AM-scaled.png?resize=2048%2C1130&amp;ssl=1 2048w, https://i0.wp.com/semiengineering.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-20-at-9.54.18-AM-scaled.png?resize=600%2C331&amp;ssl=1 600w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><br />
<strong>Fig. 4: View from the show floor. Source: SEMI</strong></p>
<p>Agentic AI will be judged by which engineering and manufacturing decisions companies are willing to let agents make, and the constraints they apply. Heterogeneous integration will put more pressure on inspection, metrology, and test to establish confidence before more value is committed to assembly. Co-packaged optics will have to move from demonstrations toward repeatable manufacturing. Alongside those, high-NA EUV is moving toward production, power delivery is moving deeper into packages, and materials suppliers are being asked to understand interface and process interactions that aren’t part of traditional specifications.</p>
<p>Three years ago, SEMICON West was talking about how the industry could reach $1 trillion by 2030. Having reached that milestone years early, the conversation has changed. The challenge is no longer just increasing density or manufacturing more chips. It&#8217;s building increasingly complex semiconductor systems fast enough, reliably enough, and economically enough to keep pace.</p>

		<link>https://semiengineering.com/how-self-aligned-cfet-technology-could-extend-cmos-scaling-beyond-10-a/</link>

		<pubDate>Thu, 22 Oct 2026 07:05:02 +0000</pubDate>
